Götterdämmerung
Götterdämmerung (Twilight of the Gods), WWV 86D, is the last of the four <color=#3366CC>epic</color> music dramas that constitute <color=#3366CC>Richard</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wagner</color>'s cycle <color=#3366CC>Der Ring des Nibelungen</color> (English: The Ring of the Nibelung). It received its premiere at the Bayreuth
Festspielhaus on 17 August 1876, as part of the first complete performance of the whole work.
The title is a German calque of the Old Norse phrase <color=#3366CC>Ragnarök</color>, which in <color=#3366CC>Norse mythology</color> refers to a prophesied war
among various beings and gods that ultimately results in the burning, immersion in water, and renewal of the world. As
with the rest of the Ring, Wagner's account diverges significantly from these Old Norse sources.
The autograph manuscript of the work is preserved in the Richard Wagner Foundation.
Composition
Roles
Synopsis
Prologue
Prelude to the Prologue
Scene 1
The three Norns, daughters of Erda, the goddess of Nature, gather beside <color=#3366CC>Brünnhilde</color>'s rock, weaving the Rope of
Destiny. From it they read of the past, the present, and of the future when <color=#3366CC>Valhalla</color> will be set on fire and the end of the
<color=#3366CC>gods</color> will come ("Welch' Licht leuchtet dort?"). As their narration approaches the point when they want to sing about the
fate of Alberich's ring and its curse and as the themes of Siegfried and the Curse of the ring are heard, the rope breaks.
Lamenting the loss of their wisdom, the Norns disappear, returning to their mother Erda beneath the earth ("Zu End'
ewiges Wissen!").
Orchestral Interlude - Tagesgrauen (Dawn)
Scene 2
As day breaks, <color=#3366CC>Siegfried</color> and Brünnhilde emerge from their dwelling high on a mountaintop surrounded by magic fire
("Zu neuen Thaten, theurer Helde"). Brünnhilde sends Siegfried off to new heroic deeds, urging him to keep their love
in mind. Siegfried proclaims himself to be simply an executor of her will, and as a pledge of his fidelity he gives her the
ring of power that he took from Fafner's hoard. In a duet, both of them extoll their loving bond, which nothing can untie,
even when distance keeps them apart ("O! heilige Götter!"). Bearing Brünnhilde's shield and mounting her steed Grane,
Siegfried then rides away.
Orchestral Interlude - Siegfrieds Rheinfahrt (Siegfried's Rhine Journey)
Act 1
Scene 1
The act begins on the shores of the <color=#3366CC>Rhine</color> in the Hall of the Gibichungs, a people named after the deceased king
Gibich. Gunther, his son and heir, sits enthroned. Gunther's half-brother and chief minister Hagen advises him to find a
wife for himself and a husband for Gutrune, the sister of them both, to enlarge the glory and might of their dynasty and
secure it for the future. He suggests Brünnhilde, the noblest of women, as appropriate for Gunther, and Siegfried, the
dragon-slayer, the greatest of heroes, as the best husband for Gutrune. Neither Gunther nor Gutrune knows how to win
themselves such partners, but Hagen reminds Gutrune that he has given her a potion she can use to make Siegfried
forget any woman he has ever seen and fall in love with her. Enamoured of Gutrune, Siegfried will then also be surely
willing to bring Brünnhilde, who sleeps on a mountaintop encircled by fire only the fearless can pass, to Gunther in
order to gain from him the permission for marriage with Gutrune. Gunther and Gutrune, not knowing that Siegfried and
Brünnhilde are actually in love with each other, agree enthusiastically with this plan.
Scene 2
Siegfried lands near the Gibichung Hall with his boat, seeking to meet Gunther, of whose fame he has heard during his
journey ("Heil, Siegfried, theurer Held!"). Gunther extends hospitality to the hero, and Gutrune offers him the potion.
Unaware of deception, Siegfried toasts Brünnhilde and their mutual love and drinks. In a while he loses his memory of
her and is struck by desire for Gutrune. Drugged, Siegfried then offers to win a wife for Gunther, who tells him about
Brünnhilde and the magic fire, which only a fearless person can cross. They swear <color=#3366CC>blood-brotherhood</color>, mixing their
blood in a drinking horn ("Blühenden Lebens labendes Blut"). Hagen holds the horn but does not join in the oath, and
the two new brothers then leave for Brünnhilde's rock. Hagen, left on guard duty, gloats that his so-called masters are
unwittingly bringing the ring to him ("Hier sitz ich zur Wacht" - Hagens Wacht - Hagen's Watch).
Orchestral Interlude
Scene 3
Meanwhile, Brünnhilde is visited on her rock by her <color=#3366CC>Valkyrie</color> sister Waltraute, who recounts that <color=#3366CC>Wotan</color> returned from
his wanderings with his spear shattered. The spear was the symbol of the god's authority and the source and
instrument of his power, carved with all the treaties through which he ruled. Unable to influence events any more, he
has ordered branches of <color=#3366CC>the World tree</color> to be piled around Valhalla by its heroes and waits in resignation for his ravens
to bring him news about the ring ("Höre mit Sinn, was ich dir sage!" - Waltraute's Monologue). Waltraute begs
Brünnhilde to return the ring to the Rhinemaidens, but Brünnhilde refuses to relinquish the pledge of Siegfried's love,
and Waltraute rides away in despair.
Crossing the ring of fire, Siegfried arrives disguised as Gunther by using the Tarnhelm and claims Brünnhilde for his
wife ("Brünnhild', ein Freier kam"). Though Brünnhilde, terrified by the appearance of an unknown man, tries to resist
him, without the divine powers she has earlier renounced for love's sake she has now nothing with which to defend
herself but the ring, which Siegfried manages to snatch cruelly from her hand during a fight, being immune to its
coercive power thanks to his fearlessness. Putting the ring on his own hand instead, Siegfried then spends the night
with Brünnhilde on her rock, placing the magic sword Nothung between them as a witness to his loyalty to Gunther and
his keeping the promise to bring Brünnhilde untouched ("Nun Nothung, zeuge du").
Act 2
Prelude to Act 2
Scene 1
As Hagen sits sleeping on night watch, his father Alberich appears and urges him to obtain the ring ("Schläfst du,
Hagen, mein Sohn?"). Hagen, barely conscious, swears to do so and Alberich vanishes with pleas for Hagen to remain
loyal to him.
Orchestral Interlude - Morgenröthe (The Blush of Dawn)
Scene 2
Siegfried arrives at dawn via Tarnhelm-magic back to the settlement of the Gibichungs, having resumed his natural
form and left Brünnhilde on a boat on the Rhine with Gunther. He explains to Gutrune how he managed to change his
form back from Gunther's just in time for Brünnhilde to not be able to recognize the deceit.
Scene 3
Hagen summons the Gibichung vassals to welcome Gunther and his bride (Hagens Ruf - Hagen's Call). He does this
by sounding the war-alarm. The vassals are surprised to learn that the occasion is not battle, but their master's wedding
and party. Hagen announces that Gunther has won himself a wife, and orders them to slay sacrificial animals so that
the gods may grant a happy marriage. The vassals are then told to defend their new queen's honour if someone were
to wrong her.
Scene 4
Gunther lands on the Rhine's shore in front of Siegfried, Gutrune, Hagen, and the assembled Gibichung men and
women and leads in a downcast Brünnhilde as his trophy. With false pomp he then triumphantly announces a double
wedding: Brünnhilde to himself, and Gutrune to Siegfried ("Brünnhild', die hehrste Frau"). Brünnhilde almost faints in
despair as she now sees her beloved, who does not even recognize her, with a different woman. However, she notices
the ring on Siegfried's hand, and realizes she has been betrayed ("Betrug! Betrug! Schändlichster Betrug!"). Declaring
publicly that the man who conquered her and took the ring was not Gunther but Siegfried in disguise she exposes
Gunther as an impostor who tried to increase his own prestige through the deeds of someone else. Filled with
unquenchable desperate rage she also denounces Siegfried and falsely accuses him of having intercourse with her
while in Gunther's form, thus breaking his blood-brotherhood with Gunther.
Siegfried denies Brünnhilde's charge, but the vassals urge him to prove his innocence by taking an oath. Hagen offers
his spear as the weapon by which Siegfried can do so. Siegfried agrees and swears upon Hagen's spear-point that he
may be killed with it if he has ever loved Brünnhilde ("Helle Wehr, heilige Waffe!"). She also seizes the spear and
swears that Siegfried may be killed with it for swearing the false oath. Once again Hagen supervises silently as others
take oaths to his advantage. The naively light-hearted Siegfried, wishing for his wedding day to be joyful, then leads
Gutrune and the bystanders exuberantly off to the wedding feast, as if nothing too significant has happened.
Orchestral Interlude
Scene 5
Brünnhilde, Hagen, and Gunther do not join the celebration and stay alone by the shore. Deeply shamed by
Brünnhilde's outburst in front of his subjects and thus threatened in his authority, Gunther agrees to Hagen's
suggestion that Siegfried must be killed in order for Gunther to regain his standing. Indeed, to see Siegfried die is
Gunther's duty, since the hero has apparently broken the sacred bond of blood-brotherhood during the night on the
rock with Brünnhilde, which betrayal condemns him by law to the rightful punishment of death. Brünnhilde, seeking
revenge for Siegfried's manifest treachery, joins the plot and tells Hagen that Siegfried would be vulnerable only to a
stab in the back. Hagen and Gunther decide to lure Siegfried on a hunting-trip and murder him. They sing a trio in
which Brünnhilde and Gunther vow in the name of Wotan, "guardian of oaths", to kill Siegfried, while Hagen repeats his
pledge to Alberich: to acquire the ring and rule the world through its power (Rache-Terzett - Vengeance Trio).
Act 3
Prelude to Act 3
Scene 1
In the woods by the bank of the Rhine, the Rhinemaidens swim playfully and sing a song to the Sun, mourning their lost
Rhine gold ("Frau Sonne sendet lichte Strahlen"). Siegfried happens by, separated from the hunting party while
searching for prey. The Rhinemaidens urge him to return the ring to the Rhine and thus avoid its curse, but he laughs
at them in heroic pride and says he prefers to die rather than bargain for his life. They swim away, predicting that
Siegfried will die this very day and that his heir, a lady, will treat them more fairly.
Scene 2
Siegfried rejoins the hunters, who include Gunther and Hagen. While resting, he sings them in high spirits a hero's song
about the adventures of his youth ("Mime hieß ein mürrischer Zwerg"), recounting his life with Mime, the forging of
Nothung, slaying the dragon Fafner and understanding the language of birds. Hagen gives him another potion, which
restores his memory, and Siegfried tells of discovering the sleeping Brünnhilde and awakening her with a kiss. Upon
hearing this, now having the apparent evidence of Siegfried's betrayal of the blood-brotherhood in front of Gunther and
his men, Hagen stabs Siegfried in the back with his spear, declares that he had avenged perjury and calmly walks
away. In his final agony Siegfried recollects the awakening of Brünnhilde and his love for her and with the memory of
blessed fear the feeling for Brünnhilde had taught him, seeing her giving him greetings in a vision, dies ("Brünnhilde!
Heilige Braut!"). His body is carried away in a solemn funeral procession that forms the interlude as the scene is
changed and recapitulates many of the themes associated with Siegfried and the Wälsungs.
Orchestral Interlude - Siegfrieds Trauermusik (Siegfried's Funeral March)
Scene 3
Back in the Gibichung Hall, Gutrune awaits Siegfried's return. Hagen arrives ahead of the funeral party. Gutrune is
devastated when Siegfried's corpse is brought in. Confronted with his sister's pain, Gunther blames Siegfried's death
on Hagen, who replies that Siegfried had incurred the penalty of his false oath. Moreover, he claims the ring on
Siegfried's finger by right of conquest. When Gunther objects, Hagen appeals to the vassals to support his lawful claim.
Gunther draws his sword but Hagen attacks and easily kills him. As he moves to take the ring, however, Siegfried's
hand rises miraculously in a threatening gesture. Hagen, as well as all present, recoil in utmost fear.
Brünnhilde, with her features as if transfigured, suddenly makes her entrance ("Schweigt eures Jammers jauchzenden
Schwall!"), having in the meantime met on the river's shores the daughters of the Rhine, who talked to her about the
ring and its curse. She proclaims Siegfried innocent, as she now recognizes that he betrayed her only due to an
intrigue, and declares that Siegfried's betrayal and death were necessary for her to become all-knowing and completely
free.
As the queen of the Gibichungs, Brünnhilde then issues orders for a huge funeral pyre for the dead hero to be
assembled by the river ("Starke Scheite schichtet mir dort"), and takes the ring from Siegfried's hand. With her eyes
turned upwards to the sky, she then, in an apostrophe, addresses Wotan, the ruler of oaths and laws, and proclaims
that the death of the free hero Siegfried has atoned for the god's guilt. Renouncing and overcoming the power of the
ring through the might of grieving love, she bequeaths it to the Rhinemaidens—who are to claim it from her own ashes
after fire has cleansed it of its curse—and declares that Wotan can finally truly rest in peace ("Mein Erbe nun nehm' ich
zu eigen"). Brünnhilde then lights the funeral pyre with a firebrand, and with "anxiously longed-for tidings", sends
Wotan's ravens home to command Loge, the god of fire that still burns on her rock, to fly to Valhalla and set it on fire
("Fliegt heim, ihr Raben!"). After a final eulogy to the dead hero, Brünnhilde, willing to be reunited with her love, mounts
her horse Grane and, as a valkyrie, rides into the flames, joining Siegfried in death.
A sequence of <color=#3366CC>leitmotifs</color> portray the fire flaring up, and the hall of the Gibichungs catching fire and collapsing. The
Rhine overflows its banks, quenching the flames, and the Rhinemaidens swim in to claim the ring. Hagen in a frenzy
tries at the last moment to stop them and seize the ring for himself, but they drag him into the depths and drown him
("Zurück vom Ring!"), the theme of the curse of the ring then being heard for the final time. As they celebrate the return
of the Rhinegold to their river and the breaking of its curse, a red glow spreads through the sky. The surviving
Gibichungs now see the interior of Valhalla with gods and heroes visible, as described by Waltraute in Act I, Scene 3. A
new fire flares up around the Hall of the Gods, hiding it from sight; the gods are consumed in flames and the curtain
falls. At the very end of the work the strains of the Liebeserlösung (redemption-through-love) leitmotif emerge.
Reactions
Robert A. Hall Jr. has analysed Götterdämmerung in terms of cultural symbolism. Hermann Danuser has discussed the
dramaturgy of the ending of Götterdämmerung in the context of the entire Ring cycle. William Kinderman has evaluated
a large-scale instance of musical recapitulation in Act III. Warren J. Darcy has expostulated on the potential influence of
Wagner's readings of the philosophy of <color=#3366CC>Arthur Schopenhauer</color> on the music of the Ring cycle, particularly on the ending
of Götterdämmerung.
The German bass Kurt Moll noted that the role of the principal villain, Hagen, is unique in the bass repertoire. It
demands a shouting, blaring vocal technique that risks damaging the singer's voice; only very large-voiced, powerful
singers can perform it. Moll himself chose to avoid the role.
<color=#3366CC>Friedrich Nietzsche</color>'s 1888–1889 book, Götzendämmerung—Twilight of the Idols—is a pun on the title of
Götterdämmerung, Götze being the German word for "idol" or "false god".

Oxalic acid
Oxalic acid is an <color=#3366CC>organic acid</color> with the systematic name ethanedioic acid and <color=#3366CC>chemical formula</color>
HO\sC(\dO)\sC(\dO)\sOH, also written as (COOH)2 or (CO2H)2 or H2C2O4. It is the simplest dicarboxylic acid. It is a
white crystalline solid that forms a colorless solution in water. Its name is derived from early investigators who isolated
oxalic acid from <color=#3366CC>flowering plants</color> of the genus Oxalis, commonly known as wood-sorrels. It occurs naturally in many
foods. It can be toxic when ingested in significant quantities, and contact with concentrated forms can cause chemical
burns.
Oxalic acid is a much stronger acid than <color=#3366CC>acetic acid</color>. It is a <color=#3366CC>reducing agent</color> and its <color=#3366CC>conjugate bases</color> hydrogenoxalate
(HC2O4) and oxalate (C2O4(2-)) are <color=#3366CC>chelating agents</color> for metal cations. It is used as a cleaning agent, especially for
the removal of <color=#3366CC>rust</color>, because it forms a water-soluble ferric iron complex, the ferrioxalate ion. Oxalic acid typically
occurs as the dihydrate with the formula H2C2O4*2H2O.
History
The preparation of salts of oxalic acid from plants had been known since at least 1745, when the Dutch botanist and
physician Herman Boerhaave isolated a salt from wood sorrel, akin to kraft process.
By 1773, François Pierre Savary of Fribourg, <color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color> had isolated oxalic acid from its salt in sorrel.
In 1776, Swedish chemists <color=#3366CC>Carl Wilhelm Scheele</color> and Torbern Olof Bergman produced oxalic acid by reacting sugar
with concentrated <color=#3366CC>nitric acid</color>; Scheele called the acid that resulted socker-syra or såcker-syra (sugar acid). By 1784,
Scheele had shown that "sugar acid" and oxalic acid from natural sources were identical. The modern name was
introduced (along with <color=#3366CC>many other acid names</color>) in 1787, by de Morveau, <color=#3366CC>Lavoisier</color> and co-authors.
In 1824, the German chemist <color=#3366CC>Friedrich Wöhler</color> obtained oxalic acid by reacting <color=#3366CC>cyanogen</color> with ammonia in aqueous
solution. This experiment may represent the first synthesis of a <color=#3366CC>natural product</color>.
Production
Industrial
Oxalic acid is mainly manufactured by the oxidation of <color=#3366CC>carbohydrates</color> like <color=#3366CC>glucose</color> using <color=#3366CC>nitric acid</color> or air in the presence
of vanadium pentoxide. Another process uses oxygen to regenerate the nitric acid, using a variety of precursors
including glycolic acid and <color=#3366CC>ethylene glycol</color>. As of 2011, this process was only used by <color=#3366CC>Mitsubishi</color> in Japan. A newer
method entails oxidative carbonylation of <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color> to give the <color=#3366CC>diesters</color> of oxalic acid:
4 ROH + 4 CO + O2 2 (CO2R)2 + 2 H2O
These diesters are subsequently hydrolyzed to oxalic acid. Approximately 120,000 <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color> are produced annually.
Historically oxalic acid was obtained exclusively by using caustics, such as <color=#3366CC>sodium</color> or <color=#3366CC>potassium hydroxide</color>, on
sawdust, followed by acidification of the oxalate by mineral acids, such as <color=#3366CC>sulfuric acid</color>. Oxalic acid can also be formed
by the heating of sodium formate in the presence of an <color=#3366CC>alkaline</color> catalyst.
Laboratory
Although it can be readily purchased, oxalic acid can be prepared in the laboratory by <color=#3366CC>oxidizing</color> <color=#3366CC>sucrose</color> using <color=#3366CC>nitric</color>
<color=#3366CC>acid</color> in the presence of a small amount of vanadium pentoxide as a <color=#3366CC>catalyst</color>.
The dihydrate can be converted to the anhydrous form by heating or <color=#3366CC>azeotropic distillation</color>.
Structure
Anhydrous
Anhydrous oxalic acid exists as two <color=#3366CC>polymorphs</color>; in one the <color=#3366CC>hydrogen-bonding</color> results in a chain-like structure, whereas
the hydrogen bonding pattern in the other form defines a sheet-like structure. Because the anhydrous material is both
acidic and <color=#3366CC>hydrophilic</color> (water seeking), it is used in <color=#3366CC>esterifications</color>.
Dihydrate
The dihydrate H2C2O4*2H2O has space group C52h–P21/n, with lattice parameters a = 611.9 pm, b = 360.7 pm, c =
1205.7 pm, = 106°19′, Z = 2. The main inter-atomic distances are: CC 153 pm, CO1 129 pm, CO2 119 pm.
Reactions
Acid–base properties
Oxalic acid's pKa values vary in the literature from 1.25 to 1.46 and from 3.81 to 4.40. The 100th ed of the CRC,
released in 2019, has values of 1.25 and 3.81. Oxalic acid is relatively strong compared to other <color=#3366CC>carboxylic acids</color>:
Oxalic acid undergoes many of the reactions characteristic for other carboxylic acids. It forms esters such as dimethyl
oxalate (<color=#3366CC>m.p.</color> 52.5 to 53.5 C). It forms an acid chloride called oxalyl chloride.
Metal-binding properties
Transition metal oxalate complexes are numerous, e.g. the drug oxaliplatin. Oxalic acid has been shown to reduce
<color=#3366CC>manganese dioxide</color> (MnO2) in manganese ores to allow the leaching of the metal by <color=#3366CC>sulfuric acid</color>.
Oxalic acid is an important reagent in <color=#3366CC>lanthanide</color> chemistry. Hydrated lanthanide oxalates form readily in very strongly
acidic solutions as a densely crystalline, easily filtered form, largely free of contamination by nonlanthanide elements: 2
Ln(3+) + 3 H2C2O4 Ln2(C2O4)3 + 6 H+ Thermal decomposition of these oxalates gives the <color=#3366CC>oxides</color>, which is the most
commonly marketed form of these elements.
Other
Oxalic acid and oxalates can be oxidized by <color=#3366CC>permanganate</color> ion in an autocatalytic reaction.
Oxalic acid vapor decomposes at 125–175 C to CO2 and <color=#3366CC>formic acid</color> (HCOOH). Photolysis with 237–313 nm <color=#3366CC>UV</color> light
also produces carbon monoxide (CO) and water.
Evaporation of a solution of <color=#3366CC>urea</color> and oxalic acid in 2:1 molar ratio yields a solid crystalline compound
H2C2O4*2CO(NH2)2, consisting of stacked two-dimensional networks of the neutral molecules held together by
<color=#3366CC>hydrogen bonds</color> with the oxygen atoms.
Occurrence
Biosynthesis
At least two pathways exist for the enzyme-mediated formation of oxalate. In one pathway, oxaloacetate, a component
of the <color=#3366CC>Krebs citric acid cycle</color>, is hydrolyzed to oxalate and acetic acid by the enzyme oxaloacetase:
[O2CC(O)CH2CO2](2) + H2O C2O4(2) + CH3CO2 + H+
It also arises from the dehydrogenation of glycolic acid, which is produced by the metabolism of <color=#3366CC>ethylene glycol</color>.
Occurrence in foods and plants
Early investigators isolated oxalic acid from wood-sorrel (Oxalis). Members of the <color=#3366CC>spinach</color> family and the brassicas

(<color=#3366CC>cabbage</color>, <color=#3366CC>broccoli</color>, <color=#3366CC>brussels sprouts</color>) are high in oxalates, as are sorrel and <color=#3366CC>umbellifers</color> like <color=#3366CC>parsley</color>. The leaves and
stems of all species of the genus Chenopodium and related genera of the family <color=#3366CC>Amaranthaceae</color>, which includes
<color=#3366CC>quinoa</color>, contain high levels of oxalic acid. <color=#3366CC>Rhubarb</color> leaves contain about 0.5% oxalic acid, and jack-in-the-pulpit
(Arisaema triphyllum) contains calcium oxalate crystals. Similarly, the Virginia creeper, a common decorative vine,
produces oxalic acid in its berries as well as oxalate crystals in the sap, in the form of raphides. Bacteria produce
oxalates from oxidation of <color=#3366CC>carbohydrates</color>.
Plants of the genus Fenestraria produce optical fibers made from crystalline oxalic acid to transmit light to subterranean
photosynthetic sites.
Carambola, also known as starfruit, also contains oxalic acid along with caramboxin. Citrus juice contains small
amounts of oxalic acid.
The formation of naturally occurring calcium oxalate patinas on certain <color=#3366CC>limestone</color> and <color=#3366CC>marble</color> statues and monuments
has been proposed to be caused by the chemical reaction of the carbonate stone with oxalic acid secreted by <color=#3366CC>lichen</color> or
other <color=#3366CC>microorganisms</color>.
Production by fungi
Many soil fungus species secrete oxalic acid, which results in greater solubility of metal cations and increased
availability of certain soil nutrients, and can lead to the formation of calcium oxalate crystals. Some fungi such as
Aspergillus niger have been extensively studied for the industrial production of oxalic acid; however, those processes
are not yet economically competitive with production from oil and gas. Cryphonectria parasitica may excrete oxalic acid
containing solutions at the advancing edge of its chestnut cambium infection. The lower pH (‹2.5) of more concentrated
oxalic acid excretions may degrade cambium cell walls and have a toxic effect on chestnut cambium cells. Cambium
cells that burst provide nutrients for a blight infection advance.
Biochemistry
The <color=#3366CC>conjugate base</color> of oxalic acid is the hydrogenoxalate anion, and its conjugate base (oxalate) is a competitive
inhibitor of the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) enzyme. LDH catalyses the conversion of pyruvate to <color=#3366CC>lactic acid</color> (end
product of the fermentation (anaerobic) process) oxidising the coenzyme <color=#3366CC>NADH</color> to <color=#3366CC>NAD+</color> and H+ concurrently.
Restoring NAD+ levels is essential to the continuation of anaerobic energy metabolism through <color=#3366CC>glycolysis</color>. As cancer
cells preferentially use anaerobic metabolism (see Warburg effect) inhibition of LDH has been shown to inhibit tumor
formation and growth, thus is an interesting potential course of cancer treatment.
Oxalic acid plays a key role in the interaction between pathogenic fungi and plants. Small amounts of oxalic acid
enhances plant resistance to fungi, but higher amounts cause widespread programmed cell death of the plant and help
with fungi infection. Plants normally produce it in small amounts, but some pathogenic fungi such as Sclerotinia
sclerotiorum cause a toxic accumulation.
Oxalate, besides being biosynthesised, may also be biodegraded. Oxalobacter formigenes is an important gut
bacterium that helps animals (including humans) degrade oxalate.
Applications
Oxalic acid's main applications include cleaning or bleaching, especially for the removal of rust (iron complexing agent).
It is the primary active ingredient in Bar Keepers Friend brand cleaner. Its utility in rust removal agents is due to its
forming a stable, water-soluble salt with ferric iron, ferrioxalate ion.
Oxalic acid is an ingredient in some tooth whitening products. About 25% of produced oxalic acid is used as a mordant
in dyeing processes. It is also used in <color=#3366CC>bleaches</color>, especially for pulpwood, cork, straw, cane, feathers, and for rust
removal and other cleaning, in baking powder, and as a third reagent in silica analysis instruments.
Niche uses
Some beekeepers use oxalic acid as a <color=#3366CC>miticide</color> against the parasitic varroa mite.
Dilute solutions (0.05–0.15 <color=#3366CC>M</color>) of oxalic acid can be used to remove iron from clays such as <color=#3366CC>kaolinite</color> to produce
light-colored <color=#3366CC>ceramics</color>.
Oxalic acid can be used to clean minerals like many other acids. Two such examples are quartz crystals and pyrite.
Oxalic acid is sometimes used in the aluminum <color=#3366CC>anodizing</color> process, with or without sulfuric acid. Compared to
sulfuric-acid anodizing, the coatings obtained are thinner and exhibit lower surface roughness.
Oxalic acid is also widely used as a wood bleach; most often it is supplied in its crystalline form, so as to be mixed with
water to its proper dilution for use.
Semiconductor industry
Oxalic acid is also used in electronic and semiconductor industries. In 2006 it was reported being used in
electrochemical–mechanical planarization of copper layers in the semiconductor devices fabrication process.
Proposed uses
Reduction of <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color> to oxalic acid by various methods, such as <color=#3366CC>electrocatalysis</color> using a <color=#3366CC>copper</color> complex, is
under study as a proposed chemical intermediate for carbon capture and utilization.
Content in food items
Toxicity
Oxalic acid has an oral LDLo (lowest published lethal dose) of 600 mg/kg. It has been reported that the lethal oral dose
is 15 to 30 grams. The toxicity of oxalic acid is due to kidney failure caused by precipitation of solid calcium oxalate.
Oxalate is known to cause mitochondrial dysfunction.
Ingestion of <color=#3366CC>ethylene glycol</color> results in oxalic acid as a metabolite which can also cause acute kidney failure.
Southern Europe
Southern Europe is a loosely defined region of <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. It is also known as Mediterranean Europe, as its geography is
marked by the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>. Southern Europe is focused on the three peninsulas located in the extreme south of
the European continent. These are the <color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Balkan Peninsula</color>. These
peninsulas are separated from the rest of Europe by towering mountain ranges, respectively by the <color=#3366CC>Pyrenees</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Alps</color>,
and the <color=#3366CC>Balkan Mountains</color>. The location of these three peninsulas in the heart of the Mediterranean Sea, as well as
their mountainous reliefs, provide them with very different types of climates (mainly <color=#3366CC>subtropical</color> <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color>) from the
rest of the continent. Moreover, these mountains have acted as a barrier to population movement and cultural
exchange, rendering both the climate and cultures distinct from those of the rest of Europe.

Various other methods can be used to define Southern Europe, including its <color=#3366CC>political</color>, <color=#3366CC>economic</color>, <color=#3366CC>historical</color>, and <color=#3366CC>cultural</color>
attributes. Culturally, Southern Europe is predominantly <color=#3366CC>Romance-speaking</color> and Roman Catholic. Politically, nine of the
southern European countries form the EU Med Group. Southern Europe also loosely corresponds to the European part
of the Mediterranean Basin.
Southern Europe has been shaped by a long and complex history rooted in the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean world</color>. Early civilizations
such as the <color=#3366CC>Phoenicians</color> established extensive trade networks that linked the region's coasts and islands. <color=#3366CC>Ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> later integrated much of Southern Europe into a shared classical framework constituting the base of
<color=#3366CC>European civilization</color>. During the Middle Ages, Southern Europe experienced centuries of political fragmentation and
external invasions. The Renaissance and the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> expanded Southern Europe's influence and global
connections, in particular to <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color>. From the late modern period onward, however, Southern Europe generally
lagged behind northern Europe in industrialization and economic development, remaining more agrarian and subject to
political instability. This gap persisted into the 20th century, despite later industrial growth and modernization driven by
state intervention and European integration.
Geography
Geographically, Southern Europe is the southern portion of the <color=#3366CC>European</color> continent. This definition is relative, although
largely based on history, culture, <color=#3366CC>climate</color>, and flora, which is shared across the region. Southern Europe is primarily
shaped by the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>, while also encompassing territories bordering the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color> to the west and
the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> to the east, as well as inland regions, often mountainous in character. Southern Europe can be
subdivided into three geographically separate subregions:
• The westernmost region (Southwest Europe), which consists mainly of the <color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color>, separated from the
rest of Europe by the <color=#3366CC>Pyrenees</color>, a mountain range forming a nearly straight line from the Atlantic Ocean to the
western Mediterranean Sea. It also consists of the <color=#3366CC>Balearic Islands</color>. The region is shared by five countries:
• <color=#3366CC>Andorra</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> (mainland)
• <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> (mainland and Balearic Islands)
• Part of <color=#3366CC>France</color>: Cerdagne in the Pyrénées-Orientales
• Part of the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>: <color=#3366CC>Gibraltar</color>
• The most central region, which consists mainly of the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color>, separated from the rest of Europe by the
<color=#3366CC>Alps</color>, a mountain range forming an arc from the western Mediterranean Sea to the <color=#3366CC>Adriatic Sea</color>. It also consists of
the islands of <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Corsica</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Malta</color>. The region is shared by nine countries:
• <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Malta</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Monaco</color>
• <color=#3366CC>San Marino</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Vatican City</color>
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color>: Istria County
• Part of <color=#3366CC>France</color>: Alpes-Maritimes and <color=#3366CC>Corsica</color>
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Slovenia</color>: municipalities of Ankaran, Izola, Koper, and Piran
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Switzerland</color>: <color=#3366CC>Ticino</color>
• The easternmost region (Southeastern Europe), a loosely defined region which consists mainly of the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, the
peninsula between the Adriatic, <color=#3366CC>Aegean</color> and Black Sea, with the <color=#3366CC>Danube</color> forming part of its northern border, rather
than the <color=#3366CC>Balkan Mountains</color> themselves (to the south). It also consists of numerous islands in the Adriatic and <color=#3366CC>in the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Aegean Sea</color> (notably <color=#3366CC>Crete</color>). The region is shared by a dozen of countries:
• <color=#3366CC>Albania</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Bosnia and Herzegovina</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Kosovo</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Montenegro</color>
• <color=#3366CC>North Macedonia</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color>
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Romania</color>: Northern Dobruja
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Slovenia</color>: southernmost part
• Part of <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>: <color=#3366CC>East Thrace</color>
Additionally, several other countries are politically or culturally associated with Southern Europe without being
geographically part of it. These include <color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color> (an island south of the <color=#3366CC>Anatolian Peninsula</color>), and <color=#3366CC>Moldova</color> (along with
the remaining part of Romania, north of the Balkan Peninsula). Further east, the coastal regions of the Black Sea and
the <color=#3366CC>Caspian Sea</color> constitute the southernmost regions of Eastern Europe, although they fall outside the core definitions
of Southern Europe.
Punta de Tarifa, in Spain, constitutes the southernmost point of the European continent. Gavdos, in Greece, is the
southernmost European island.
Climate
Southern Europe's most emblematic <color=#3366CC>climate</color> is the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean climate</color>, influenced by the large subtropical
semi-permanent centre of high atmospheric pressure found, not in the Mediterranean itself, but in the Atlantic Ocean,
the Azores High. The Mediterranean climate covers <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, the southern coast of France, coastal

<color=#3366CC>Croatia</color>, coastal <color=#3366CC>Slovenia</color>, southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, <color=#3366CC>Montenegro</color>, <color=#3366CC>Albania</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>, as well as the
Mediterranean islands. Those areas of Mediterranean climate present similar vegetation and landscapes throughout,
including dry hills, small plains, <color=#3366CC>pine</color> forests, and <color=#3366CC>olive</color> trees.
Cooler climates can be found in certain parts of southern European countries, for example, within the mountain ranges
of Spain and Italy. Additionally, the north coast of Spain experiences a wetter Atlantic climate. In the highest regions of
the Alps, which border southern Europe, even an ice cap climate can be found.
Some parts of southern Europe have humid subtropical climates with warm and wet summers, unlike typical
Mediterranean climates. This climate is mainly found in Italy and Croatia around the <color=#3366CC>Adriatic Sea</color> in cities such as
<color=#3366CC>Venice</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color>, but also further north, near the Alpine foothills, in cities such as Como and Lugano.
The high mountains of the Alps and the Pyrenees act as a significant <color=#3366CC>climatic barrier</color>. An example is the Sirocco, a hot
wind that originates in the heart of the <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color> and blows over Italy as far as the interior of the Alpine arc (the Po
Valley), where it is prevented from spreading to the rest of Europe. Conversely, the Alps and the Pyrenees protect the
Italian and Iberian peninsulas from the rain and icy winds coming from southern France, such as the Mistral and the
Tramontane. When the Mistral and the Tramontane are blowing, they provoke an <color=#3366CC>upwelling</color> phenomenon along the
French coast: surface waters are pushed offshore, allowing deeper, cooler waters to rise to the surface near the shore.
Consequently, water temperatures along the French coast remain very cool even in summer and are not representative
of the rest of the Mediterranean. This same kind of phenomenon takes place between the two slopes of the Balkan
mountain range.
Flora
Southern Europe's flora is mainly characterized by <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean forests, woodlands, and scrub</color>, but also <color=#3366CC>temperate</color>
<color=#3366CC>broadleaf and mixed forests</color>. The Mediterranean and Submediterranean climate regions in Europe are found in much of
southern Europe, mainly Portugal, Spain, Italy, Malta, Albania, Greece, Cyprus and all the mediterranean islands, but
also in southeast France and the <color=#3366CC>Balkan</color> Mediterranean coast.
In the Mediterranean coastal areas, <color=#3366CC>olive groves</color>, maquis shrubland, and <color=#3366CC>steppes</color> are very common. At higher
elevations, or latitudes, they are replaced by <color=#3366CC>chestnut</color> and (often coppiced) mixed forests.
History
Early history

The <color=#3366CC>Phoenicians</color> originally expanded from <color=#3366CC>Canaan</color> <color=#3366CC>ports</color>, dominating trade in the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> by the 8th century BC.
<color=#3366CC>Carthage</color> was founded in 814 BC, and the <color=#3366CC>Carthaginians</color> by 700 BC had firmly established strongholds in <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Sardinia</color> (both regions in present day <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>), which created conflicts of interest with Etruria. Its colonies later reached the

<color=#3366CC>Western Mediterranean</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>Cádiz</color> in Spain and most notably <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color> in North Africa, and even the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ocean</color>. The civilisation spread across the Mediterranean between 1500 BC and 300 BC.
The period known as <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> began with the rise of the city-states of <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greece</color>. Greek influence
reached its zenith under the expansive empire of <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color>, spreading throughout <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>
came to dominate the entire Mediterranean Basin in a vast empire based on <color=#3366CC>Roman law</color> and <color=#3366CC>Roman legions</color>. It
promoted trade, tolerance, and Greek culture. By 300 AD the Roman Empire was divided into the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> based in Rome, and the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> based in Constantinople. The attacks of the <color=#3366CC>Goths</color> led to the
<color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> in 476 AD, a date that traditionally marks the end of the classical period and the start
of the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>. During the Middle Ages, the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> survived though modern historians refer to the
state as the Byzantine Empire. In Western Europe, <color=#3366CC>Germanic peoples</color> moved into positions of power in the remnants of
the former Western Roman Empire and established kingdoms and empires of their own.
The period known as the <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color>, a series of religiously-motivated military expeditions originally intended to bring the
<color=#3366CC>Levant</color> back into Christian rule, began. Several <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color> were founded in the eastern Mediterranean, but they
were all short-lived. The Crusaders would have a profound impact on many parts of Europe. Their <color=#3366CC>sack of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> in 1204 brought an abrupt end to the Byzantine Empire. Though it would later be re-established, it
would never recover its former glory. The Crusaders would establish trade routes that would develop into the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color>
and open the way for the merchant republics of <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venice</color> to become major economic powers. The

<color=#3366CC>Reconquista</color>, a related movement, worked to reconquer <color=#3366CC>Iberia</color> for <color=#3366CC>Christendom</color>. The <color=#3366CC>late Middle Ages</color> represented a
period of upheaval in Europe. The epidemic known as the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> and an associated famine caused <color=#3366CC>demographic</color>
catastrophe in Europe as the population plummeted. Dynastic struggles and <color=#3366CC>wars of conquest</color> kept many of the states
of Europe at war for much of the period. In the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>, a Turkish state originating in <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>,
encroached steadily on former Byzantine lands, culminating in the <color=#3366CC>fall of Constantinople</color> in 1453.
Post-Middle Ages
Beginning roughly in the 12th century in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, and later spreading through Europe with the development of the
<color=#3366CC>printing press</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> of knowledge challenged traditional doctrines in science and <color=#3366CC>theology</color>, with the Arabic
texts and thought bringing about rediscovery of classical Greek and Roman knowledge. The Catholic reconquest of
Portugal and Spain led to a series of oceanic explorations resulting in the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> that established direct links
with Africa, the Americas, and Asia. During this period, Iberian forces engaged in a worldwide struggle with Islamic
societies; the battlefronts in this Ibero-Islamic World War stretched from the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> into the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color>,
finally involving the islands of <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> (see also: Indo-Mediterranean). Eventually this ecumenical conflict ended
when new players—England, Holland and France—replaced Spain and Portugal as the main agents of European
imperialism in the mid-17th century.
European overseas expansion led to the rise of colonial empires, producing the <color=#3366CC>Columbian Exchange</color>. <color=#3366CC>Most of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Americas</color> inherited two of Southern Europe’s main languages: Spanish and Portuguese. The combination of resource
inflows from the New World and the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> of Great Britain, allowed a new economy based on
manufacturing instead of subsistence agriculture. The period between 1815 and 1871 saw a large number of
revolutionary attempts and independence wars. Balkan nations began to regain independence from the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>. Italy unified into a nation state. The capture of Rome in 1870 ended the Papal temporal power.
19th to 21st century
Mountainous terrain and fragmented coastlines hindered Southern Europe’s industrialization. During the 19th century,
countries such as Spain, Portugal, Italy, and Greece remained predominantly agrarian, with industrial growth
concentrated in only a few urban regions (notably northern Italy and Catalonia). Political instability in the Iberian
Peninsula and the Balkans, along with the influence of organized crime in Italy, further undermined economic
development throughout much of the 20th century.
The outbreak of <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> in 1914 was precipitated by the rise of nationalism in Southeastern Europe as the <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Powers</color> took up sides. The Allies defeated the <color=#3366CC>Central Powers</color> in 1918. During the <color=#3366CC>Paris Peace Conference</color> the Big
Four imposed their terms in a series of treaties, especially the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Versailles</color>. The Nazi regime under <color=#3366CC>Adolf Hitler</color>
came to power in 1933, and along with <color=#3366CC>Mussolini's Italy</color> sought to gain control of the continent by the <color=#3366CC>Second World</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color>. Following the Allied victory in the Second World War, Europe was divided by the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color>. The countries in
Eastern and Southeastern Europe were dominated by the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and became communist states. The major
non-communist southern European countries joined a US-led military alliance (<color=#3366CC>NATO</color>) and formed the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>Economic Community</color> amongst themselves. The countries in the Soviet sphere of influence joined the military alliance
known as the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> and the economic bloc called <color=#3366CC>Comecon</color>. Yugoslavia was neutral. The common attribute of
the eastern countries is that all of them have experiences with <color=#3366CC>socialism</color>, but nevertheless, the beginning of the 1990s
was just roughly the same. For some of them becoming independent was the major challenge, while others needed to
face with poverty and deep dictatorship also Economically, parallel with the political changes, and the democratic
transition, – as a rule of law states – the previous command economies were transformed via the legislation into market
economies, and set up or renewed the major macroeconomic factors: budgetary rules, national audit, national currency,
central bank. Generally, they shortly encountered the following problems: high inflation, high unemployment, low
economic growth and high government debt. By 2000 these economies were stabilized, and sooner or later between
2004 and 2013 some of them joined the European Union, and Slovenia introduced the euro.
Italy became a major <color=#3366CC>industrialized country</color> again because of its post-war economic miracle. The <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> (EU)
involved the division of powers; <color=#3366CC>tax</color>, health and education handled by the nation states, and the EU had charge of
market rules, competition, legal standards and environmentalism. The Soviet economic and political system collapsed,
leading to the end of communism in the satellite countries in 1989 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself in 1991.
The European Union expanded to subsequently include many of the formerly communist European countries –
<color=#3366CC>Romania</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color> (2007) and <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color> (2013).
The Gotthard, a major and direct transport axis between northern and Southern Europe, was completed in 2016 with
the <color=#3366CC>Gotthard Base Tunnel</color>. The Gotthard inscribes itself in a long history of transit across the Alps, which saw them
progressively changing from an obstacle to a corridor between the <color=#3366CC>North Sea</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>.
Demographics
Languages
Romance languages
The most widely spoken family of languages in southern Europe are the <color=#3366CC>Romance languages</color>, the heirs of Latin, which
have spread from the Italian peninsula, and are emblematic of Southwestern Europe (See the Latin Arch.). By far the
most common Romance languages in southern Europe are <color=#3366CC>Italian</color> (spoken by over 50 million people in Italy, southern
Switzerland, Malta, San Marino, and Vatican City) and <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, which is spoken by over 40 million people in Spain,
Andorra and Gibraltar. Other common Romance languages include <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> (spoken in Portugal), <color=#3366CC>French</color> (spoken
in France, Monaco, and the <color=#3366CC>Aosta Valley</color> in Italy), <color=#3366CC>Catalan</color> (spoken in eastern Spain, Andorra, Southwestern France,
and the <color=#3366CC>Sardinian</color> town of Alghero in Italy), <color=#3366CC>Galician</color> (spoken in northwestern Spain), Mirandese (spoken in northeast
Portugal), and <color=#3366CC>Occitan</color>, which is spoken in the Val d'Aran in Catalonia, in the Occitan Valleys in Italy and in southern
France.
Slavic languages

Religion
The predominant religion in southern Europe is <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>. Christianity spread throughout southern Europe during the
Roman Empire, and Christianity was adopted as the official religion of the Roman Empire in the year 380 AD. The
<color=#3366CC>historic break of the Church</color> into the western half, based in <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, and the eastern half, based in <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color>, has
caused different denominations of Christianity to be prominent in different parts of Europe. <color=#3366CC>Christians</color> in the western
half of southern Europe such as Portugal, Spain and Italy, are generally <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic</color>. Christians in the eastern half
of southern Europe such as Greece, Serbia and North Macedonia are generally <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color>. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> is widely
practiced in Albania, Bosnia, Kosovo and Turkey and <color=#3366CC>Northern Cyprus</color>. Muslims are a significant minority in several
countries of southern Europe such as Greece, Italy, Spain. <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color> was practiced widely throughout the European
continent within the Roman Empire from the 2nd century.
